A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable text, equations, figures, references, and appendices. The original theory and experiments can be matched reliably despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original embedding analyses and Llama-2-7B DPO experiments, including training/test reward margins, losses, and accuracies.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D retain those empirical results and add embedding diagnostics and Llama-3.1-8B training/test results.

M1.justification: The DPO procedure, model decomposition, and reward-dynamics approach are retained. The explicit gradient-descent equation elaborates the existing analysis; evaluating Llama-3.1-8B introduces no new proposed algorithm or component.

E1.justification: Both versions use the Anthropic Persona corpus and the same preference-learning task. The risk-aversion visualization examines the retained persona domain, and the additional model does not introduce another dataset or task.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically compares DPO against another preference-optimization algorithm. GPO and SimPO remain theoretical discussion only; Llama-3.1-8B supplies additional DPO verification rather than an alternative-method baseline.

E3.justification: v3 adds evaluation with Llama-3.1-8B using the stated Llama-2 training setup, plus normalized-embedding dispersion diagnostics. The retained experiments keep their 90/10 split, five cluster-count settings, AdamW optimizer, learning rate, and batch size.

E4.justification: v3 adds a risk-aversion embedding case study in Figure 2 and a within-cluster dispersion check in Appendix D. It also repeats the cluster-count sensitivity analysis on Llama-3.1-8B. These extend the existing assumption and robustness checks without replacing their central questions.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies experimental seeds or repeated-run counts, or reports error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added embedding-dispersion measurements characterize the data rather than uncertainty in the training results.

E6.justification: v3 substantially expands reported results with a complete Llama-3.1-8B training/test suite for reward margin, loss, and accuracy across all five cluster counts (Figures 8–10). It also adds the UMAP visualization and mean covariance Frobenius norm 0.058 and mean squared distance 0.227. Original plotted results are retained; the new model results are not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The background RLHF objective changes from v1 Equation 3 to v3 Equation 2, placing reward and the log-ratio penalty together inside an expectation over prompts. Equations 8 and 10 correct the free reward index from i to j. The main bounds, distribution assumptions, and appendix proofs remain unchanged; the beyond-DPO formulas are relocated.

C1.justification: The contribution list qualifies the novelty claim as the first comprehensive analysis of finite-step preference learning, whereas v1 states preference learning more generally. The principal DPO guarantees and empirical-validation claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 explains positive reward margins relative to the reference model and interprets small embedding dispersion as supporting Gaussian modeling. Conversely, the rewritten setup removes v1's explicit statement that the initial theory focuses on a fixed encoder. The new Limitations section largely restates the existing beyond-DPO qualification.

D1.justification: Section 3 newly documents the statement prompt template and Yes/No response mapping. Appendix D describes normalization and dispersion calculations and states that the additional model uses the existing training setup. Original optimizer, split, selected-persona, hardware, and runtime information is retained.

R1.justification: Four works are added: Chen et al. and Zhu et al. on preference-based reinforcement learning, and Hardt et al. and Liu et al. on algorithmic stability. Section 7 distinguishes offline preference optimization from those reinforcement-learning settings and acknowledges existing step-dependent stability bounds. The original references are retained.

P1.justification: v3 adds a substantial motivating-example section, rewrites and reorganizes the model/setup and dynamics exposition, moves Future Extension Beyond DPO from main Section 6 to Appendix C, and adds a separate Limitations section. These changes substantially restructure the narrative despite retaining the main scientific framework.

P2.justification: v3 adds a task schematic and UMAP visualization (Figures 1–2), plus three paired Llama-3.1-8B result figures (Figures 8–10). The original five figures survive as Figures 3–7 with placement and some caption/panel-label changes. This substantially expands the visual exposition and empirical displays.

improvement.justification: The motivating example, explicit task format, clearer gradient-flow explanation, and more precise related-work positioning improve accessibility and interpretation. Llama-3.1-8B results provide additional support for the retained empirical trend. These are limited gains: the main theoretical guarantees remain unchanged, the fixed-encoder caveat becomes less explicit, and the new dispersion statistics alone do not establish Gaussianity.
